newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Nobel award given to fiery Timorese priest.
newsitem.headline: Nobel award given to fiery Timorese priest.

text.p: East Timor's Catholic Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo, awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday, has walked a tightrope between the territory's Jakarta-appointed government and his frustrated people.
The fiery priest was saying mass in a school in East Timor's capital, Dili, when the announcement was made that he and and resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta had shared the 1996 prize.
Belo, born in Baucau, East Timor, in February 1946, was ordained in July 1980 in Lisbon and returned a year later to take up a teaching position in his home town.
It is said that it was during this period that he developed a close affinity to the youth of East Timor who now are in the vanguard of anti-Jakarta dissidence and won their respect.
He was appointed apostolic administrator of the diocese of the East Timor capital of Dili, in May 1983.
"Bishop Belo's rapid rise came as a surprise to some, who might have thought of others for such positions," Australian Catholic Bishop Hilton Deakin wrote in 1994.

"But he brought a kind and youthful personality to the position, a flair for languages, with the mastery of Tetum, Portuguese, English, Italian, Bahasa Indonesia and a working knowledge of several others," Deakin wrote.
"He also had experience in ecclesiastical administration, a love of theology and classical music and a passion for soccer."

Belo's presence as an observer at U.N.-sponsored talks between long-time warring East Timorese factions proved crucial in the first dialogue, held in Austria in June, 1995, to include all the various parties.

The talks, part of two U.N. initiatives to solve the problems surrounding East Timor's status, were the first meetings between pro- and anti-integration groups in exile since Indonesia's invasion of the territory.
Belo declined an invitation to attend a second round of talks this year on the grounds that he was busy with preparations for the celebration of Easter.
In February 1989, a time when access to East Timor was still restricted, Belo wrote a letter to the U.N. secretary-general asking for a U.N-sponsored referendum on self-determination.
While he has often spoken out against Indonesia's sometimes harsh rule in East Timor, he has equally called for the restless youth in the territory to stop fighting.
Indonesian security officials regularly call him to the scene of disputes by to help to calm unrest, while his seaside residence in Dili is often used as a refuge.
He was in the firing line last year after the Indonesian press misreported him as calling for East Timor to be declared a special Catholic area. He denied the report, saying he had been misquoted.
